strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem—mitigating inherited biases/noise during PEFT—and offers an intuitive three-way decomposition (Knowledge Drift, Representation Collapse, Overfitting to Noise) with correspondingly named regularizers (consistency, diversity, SVD), tailored separately for NLU and NLG settings.

Extensive empirical coverage: GLUE (DeBERTa-v3, RoBERTa, T5), NLG benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP, MT-Bench) on LLaMA-2-7B, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, rank sweep, and a broad model-scale/architecture study (7B–70B, dense and MoE) plus quantized variants.

The controlled RoBERTa-vs-T5 (clean vs. noisy pretraining corpus) experiment and the t-SNE/silhouette analysis under class imbalance are nice qualitative attempts to directly probe the paper's central hypothesis rather than relying solely on leaderboard numbers.

Ablation study (Table 4) and cross-method generality study (Table 10, applying the regularizers to vanilla LoRA/DoRA) support that each regularizer contributes positively and that the framework is not tightly coupled to PiSSA initialization alone.
Reasonably detailed appendix documentation of hyperparameters and settings aids reproducibility of the core NLU/NLG experiments.
weaknesses: Several reported gains look implausibly large or inconsistent with the rest of the results: e.g., BA-LoRA's MBPP score jumps from 24.74 (CorDA++) to 36.86 (+12.1 points), dwarfing the ~1-point gains seen on GSM8K/MATH/HumanEval; this outlier is never explained and raises concerns about correctness or cherry-picking.

The large-scale study across 10 models up to LLaMA-3-70B, Mixtral-8x7B, and Yi-1.5-34B (Appendix C.3) is presented only as bar charts without numerical tables, error bars, or details on how such large models were fine-tuned on stated "NVIDIA A40 GPUs" hardware; this raises reproducibility and plausibility concerns given the compute described elsewhere in the paper.

The mapping from the three named failure modes to their operationalized loss functions (batch logit decorrelation for "representation collapse", top-k singular value ratio of the logit matrix for "overfitting to noise") is heuristic and only loosely justified theoretically; the paper offers little formal analysis of why these output-space penalties specifically address the claimed underlying phenomena beyond intuitive appeals to prior work in unrelated settings (VICReg, batch spectral penalization).

The central "noisy vs. clean pretraining" experiment (RoBERTa vs. T5) confounds pretraining corpus quality with architecture, objective, tokenizer, and scale differences, weakening the causal claim that gains are specifically attributable to inherited noise mitigation rather than other model differences (e.g., the anomalously low T5+LoRA MRPC score of 68.38 vs. ~85-95 for other metrics suggests instability rather than a clean comparison).

Most NLG and NLU baseline numbers are directly copied from other papers rather than reproduced under the authors' own controlled pipeline, risking inconsistencies in evaluation protocol, data splits, or seeds that could bias the comparison in BA-LoRA's favor.

Some claims are stated with more confidence than evidence supports, e.g., "first to propose a concrete, multi-faceted algorithmic framework" for PEFT bias mitigation, and rhetorical framing ("Minimal Intervention Principle," "guided exploration within a trusted neighborhood") that is more narrative than rigorously substantiated.

No statistical significance testing is provided despite small numeric gaps between methods (e.g., ablation deltas of ~0.3-0.6 points), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust to noise given only 3 seeds.

Limited discussion of additional computational overhead when the SVD/diversity regularizers are applied to very large vocabularies or at the 34B/70B model scale, despite Table 5 only benchmarking a single 7B configuration.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: whether LoRA-style PEFT methods can amplify biases/noise inherited from pretraining data, an underexplored angle relative to the extensive LoRA-variant literature focused purely on task performance.

The proposed decomposition into three failure modes (Knowledge Drift, Representation Collapse, Overfitting to Noise) gives a clean, interpretable structure for designing regularizers, and the method is described with full mathematical detail for both NLU and NLG variants.

The empirical evaluation is broad: GLUE (8 tasks), math/code/chat NLG benchmarks, a RoBERTa-vs-T5 noisy-pretraining controlled comparison, t-SNE visualizations under class imbalance, ablations of each regularizer, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, a 'generality' study applying the regularizers on top of vanilla LoRA/DoRA, and additional appendix experiments across 10 model architectures/scales and quantized variants.

Computational overhead is reported and shown to be modest relative to PiSSA, and the paper includes a training-loss convergence comparison suggesting the regularizers also aid optimization dynamics, not just final accuracy.
The paper is generally well-written, and the appendix provides substantial implementation details (hyperparameters per task/model) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the consistency regularizer is standard (self-)knowledge distillation, the diversity regularizer is a direct application of VICReg-style covariance decorrelation (NLU) or top-k entropy maximization (NLG), and the SVD regularizer is standard spectral/low-rank regularization on logits — the main novelty is combining these three existing techniques with PiSSA initialization rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Most NLG and NLU baseline numbers are not reproduced by the authors but are taken directly from other papers (CorDA, Kang & Yin, etc.), which risks inconsistencies in data splits, prompts, decoding settings, and evaluation harnesses; only BA-LoRA (and PiSSA in some tables) appears to be run by the authors under possibly different conditions, weakening the 'fair comparison' claim.

Some reported gains look anomalously large and inconsistent with the rest of the pattern (e.g., MBPP jumps from 24.74 to 36.86, a >12-point/49% relative improvement, while GSM8K and HumanEval gains over the same strongest baseline are only 0.8–1.8 points), which is not discussed or explained and raises concerns about cherry-picking, a possible evaluation artifact, or an error.

Despite being framed as 'bias mitigation' and 'fairness,' the paper never evaluates social/demographic bias (e.g., no StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs, BBQ, or similar fairness benchmarks); the actual evidence offered (noisy-pretraining-corpus comparison, class-imbalance t-SNE plots, GLUE accuracy) measures robustness/generalization under data imbalance or noise rather than bias in the fairness sense, so the framing somewhat overstates what is empirically demonstrated.

The RoBERTa-vs-T5 'controlled' study confounds pretraining-data quality with architecture and pretraining objective differences (MLM vs. denoising T2T), so attributing the larger BA-LoRA gain on T5 specifically to noise mitigation (rather than architecture-specific characteristics) is not rigorously isolated.

The extensive appendix experiments (10 models up to 70B/MoE, quantized variants, rank sweeps) are presented with only aggregate bar charts and no per-run variance, exact numbers, or detailed protocol, making it hard to verify these claims; the sheer scale of claimed experiments (LLaMA-3-70B, Mixtral-8x7B, Yi-1.5-34B, etc., under both full and quantized 4-bit settings) also raises reproducibility and resource-transparency concerns given the compute described (2xA40 GPUs) in the main paper.

Some individual metrics do not favor BA-LoRA (e.g., MT-Bench is lower than CorDA++, STS-B/AdaLoRA comparisons are close), and the paper does not report statistical significance tests despite using multiple seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust rather than within noise, especially for smaller-magnitude gains.

The claim of being 'the first to propose a concrete, multi-faceted algorithmic framework' for mitigating bias in PEFT is a strong claim that is not thoroughly substantiated against the broader (if full fine-tuning focused) bias-mitigation literature, and related PEFT-fairness work (e.g., Ding et al., 2024) is only briefly mentioned without deeper comparison or empirical benchmarking against it.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning NLG (math reasoning, coding, conversation) and NLU (GLUE) tasks, across a wide range of backbones (LLaMA-2-7B/13B, LLaMA-3-8B/70B, Mistral, Mixtral, DeBERTa-v3, RoBERTa, T5) and against many strong recent LoRA variants (AdaLoRA, DoRA, MiLoRA, LoRA+, LoRA-FA, LoRA-GA, PiSSA, CorDA/CorDA++).

The decomposition of 'Catastrophic Inheritance' into three interpretable sub-problems (Knowledge Drift, Representation Collapse, Overfitting to Noise), each addressed by a regularizer grounded in established techniques (knowledge distillation, VICReg-style decorrelation, spectral/low-rank regularization), gives the method a clear and well-motivated structure.

Thorough ablations (per-regularizer contributions, generality across LoRA/DoRA/PiSSA, hyperparameter sensitivity, rank sweep, quantized variants) supporting the claimed synergy of the three components.

Multiple complementary lines of evidence for bias/robustness claims beyond leaderboard numbers: t-SNE visualizations with silhouette scores, minority-class recall under imbalance, RoBERTa-vs-T5 noise comparison, and Wikitext-2 perplexity to check preservation of pre-trained behavior.
Reasonable attention to computational cost and reproducibility (memory/time comparisons, complexity analysis, detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix).
weaknesses: Baseline numbers in the two main tables (NLG and NLU) are taken directly from other papers rather than reproduced under an identical pipeline by the authors; while the paper claims a 'matched setup,' this practice risks inconsistencies in hardware, tuning effort, and evaluation harnesses that could bias comparisons in BA-LoRA's favor.

The MBPP result (36.86 vs. next-best 24.74, a ~12-point jump) is a striking outlier relative to the much smaller margins on all other NLG benchmarks (≤2 points), and largely drives the reported average improvement over CorDA++; the paper offers only a brief post-hoc explanation without deeper investigation, raising concerns about its validity or an experimental artifact.

The central 'noisy pre-training' hypothesis is tested using RoBERTa-base vs. T5-base, which differ not only in pre-training corpus quality but also in architecture (encoder-only vs. encoder-decoder) and pre-training objective; the authors acknowledge this confound but the main text still presents the result as fairly strong supporting evidence for the hypothesis.

The methodological novelty is moderate: the three regularizers are largely adaptations of well-known techniques (KD-based consistency, VICReg-style covariance decorrelation, spectral/SVD-based truncation) applied to PEFT output logits, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Non-trivial additional memory/compute overhead (e.g., +10.75GB, +31min vs. PiSSA on a single setting) is reported for only one configuration; scaling behavior of the regularizers (especially the SVD term on large vocabularies) is not empirically stress-tested across settings despite asymptotic complexity claims.

Some inconsistencies/minor issues in reported statistics (e.g., silhouette score for BA-LoRA balanced setting differs slightly between Figure 3 caption and surrounding text) suggest limited quality control in reporting.

No statistical significance testing is provided despite reporting standard deviations, and in at least one benchmark (MT-Bench) a baseline (CorDA++) outperforms BA-LoRA, which is honestly reported but slightly undercuts the 'consistently outperforms' framing used elsewhere.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning NLG (math reasoning, coding, conversational) and NLU (GLUE) tasks, multiple backbones (LLaMA-2-7B, DeBERTa-v3-base, RoBERTa-base, T5-base) and comparison against a large and current set of strong LoRA-variant baselines (LoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, MiLoRA, LoRA+, LoRA-FA, LoRA-GA, PiSSA, CorDA, CorDA++).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each of the three regularizers, plus a 'generality' study showing the regularization framework also improves vanilla LoRA and DoRA, not just PiSSA.

Extensive supplementary analyses: hyperparameter sensitivity, cross-architecture/scale study (7B to 70B, dense and MoE), rank-sweep analysis, quantized (4-bit) evaluation, perplexity preservation on Wikitext-2, and quantitative cluster-quality/minority-recall metrics complementing the t-SNE visualizations.

The core idea of decomposing 'Catastrophic Inheritance' into three interpretable sub-problems (Knowledge Drift, Representation Collapse, Overfitting to Noise) and mapping each to a targeted regularizer gives the method a clear narrative and testable structure.
Results are reported with means and standard deviations over multiple seeds, and computational overhead is explicitly quantified, giving a reasonably transparent cost-benefit picture.
Good engagement with related work and an honest discussion of limitations (e.g., explicitly noting the RoBERTa/T5 comparison is confounded by architecture/objective, not just corpus quality).
weaknesses: The individual regularizers (KD-based consistency, VICReg-style covariance diversity, spectral/SVD regularization) are largely adaptations of existing techniques from other areas (self-distillation, self-supervised learning, domain adaptation); the main novelty is their combination and application to PEFT output space, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

The central causal claim -- that BA-LoRA's benefit scales with pre-training data noisiness -- rests on a RoBERTa-vs-T5 comparison that the authors themselves acknowledge is confounded by architecture (encoder-only vs. encoder-decoder) and pre-training objective (MLM vs. denoising), weakening the paper's headline hypothesis test.

The large, disproportionate gain on MBPP (36.86 vs. 24.74 for CorDA++, roughly a 12-point jump) stands out as an outlier relative to more modest 1-2 point gains on other NLG benchmarks; the explanation offered (small benchmark, prone to overfitting) is post-hoc and not independently verified, raising concern about whether this specific result is representative or an artifact of evaluation/harness differences.

Baseline numbers for NLG and NLU are taken directly from prior publications (Yang et al. 2025; Kang & Yin 2025) rather than uniformly re-run in-house alongside BA-LoRA, which, despite claimed alignment of core hyperparameters, introduces potential inconsistencies in exact data splits, prompts, or evaluation harnesses that are hard to fully control for.

Regularization coefficients differ substantially between NLU and NLG settings and are selected via per-setting grid search on held-out data, somewhat undercutting the practicality/plug-and-play appeal, despite the appendix's attempt to offer general tuning guidelines.

The three-way decomposition of Catastrophic Inheritance, while intuitively appealing, is not derived from a rigorous theoretical framework and their claimed mutual exclusivity/completeness is asserted rather than formally justified.
Memory overhead (~17% increase) and training time overhead are non-trivial, and while acknowledged, the trade-off analysis could benefit from additional baselines at matched compute budgets.
